record.paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
record.context_brief: Measurements needed to break model degeneracy
record.original_question: How should accurate gravity-field, magnetic-field, atmospheric-composition, rotation-rate, Bond-albedo, and thermal-flux measurements be combined to break the degeneracy of Uranus and Neptune interior and evolution models, rather than relying on any single precise observation?

evidence.quote: Although the development of new theoretical models is crucial, it is clear that significant progress in our knowledge cannot be achieved without more data. We argue that missions to Uranus and Neptune are essential.

In particular we emphasize the importance of accurate measurements of the planets' gravitational fields (preferable with several Juno-like polar orbits). Better gravity data will allow us to exclude certain solutions for the interiors, and can assist us in understanding the differences between Uranus and Neptune.

In addition, determining the rotation rates of the planets helps to tighten constraints on interior models. Better establishing each planet's Bond albedo and thermal fluxes can be used to further constrain structure and evolution models, respectively.

Due to the complex nature of planets, it is clear that having one measurement, even if very accurate, is insufficient to break the degeneracy of structure models and reveal the true nature of the planets.

artifact.status_search_result: The problem of jointly inverting interior and evolution models of Uranus and Neptune from combined gravity, magnetic, compositional, rotational, albedo and thermal-flux data remains open. Current studies continue to call for new spacecraft missions (e.g., NASA's Uranus Orbiter and Probe recommended by the 2023 Planetary Science Decadal Survey) precisely because existing data leave interior models highly degenerate; no published joint-inversion framework has resolved the degeneracy.

status_evidence.title: Origins, Worlds, and Life: A Decadal Strategy for Planetary Science 2023–2032
status_evidence.snippet: Recommends a Uranus Orbiter and Probe as the highest-priority new flagship mission, citing the need for gravity, magnetic, compositional and atmospheric data to constrain interior structure.
status_evidence.claim: The interior structure of Uranus/Neptune remains under-constrained and requires new combined measurements; no decisive inversion exists.

status_evidence.title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
status_evidence.snippet: Argues that combinations of gravity, magnetic, compositional, rotation, albedo and thermal-flux measurements are needed because no single observation breaks the degeneracy of interior and evolution models.
status_evidence.claim: The joint inversion question is posed as an open challenge.
